findings.text: The first lines tell a newcomer what Athena is and what sets it apart: it shows how it read the request, uses a second model to check the work, and records costs. That answers "what is this" right away.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page explains why it exists and why it matters before the detail starts. A newcomer knows the firstmate content is a demonstration, not Athena's own documentation.
findings.source: Header lede: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: A link at the top lets a newcomer skip the long study and go straight to the action. Without it the next step would be lost below about 44 claims.
findings.source: Header: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" linking to #next-steps

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout, gives no clone command, and lists no prerequisites. It does not say whether a Rust toolchain or AI model API keys are needed, so a newcomer may get stuck before the try-it command works.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: Athena gets three sentences, and almost all of the rest is about another project. A newcomer who wants to know who Athena is for, or what using it looks like and costs, has to leave for the GitHub repository.
findings.source: Header lede and title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: The walkthrough meant as the easy entry point already uses script exit codes and terms like "place" and "spawn". "Place" and "spawn" are not in the "Words used first" list above it; they are defined only in the Glossary at the end.
findings.source: "One piece of work, start to finish", step 2: "If every place of a declared capacity is held, the spawn exits 75 and the item stays queued."

findings.text: The page openly admits what its sources do not support, here and under "Limits of this study" ("every claim is marked read", none run). This builds trust in the traceability promise, but it adds caveats a newcomer has to read through.
findings.source: Words used first: "in scope ... The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: The page tells readers how to check its own claims, and every claim links to file and line ranges at the pinned commit. This gives concrete proof of what the header promises.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
